turns.name: Peter Salib
turns.text:
I come to "who gets paid" from a copyright and law-and-economics angle, and my answer will be unpopular here. Copyright isn't a welfare program. Its job is to create incentives for new ideas. It was never meant to guarantee creators a fair share of whatever someone later builds from their work.

Yes, the fairness complaint is factually true: models were built on decades of human writing. But copyright law has always allowed that kind of unfairness. Making AI training an infringement, or putting a levy on it, would probably reduce the net number of new ideas, because ideas are non-rival and every IP restriction causes social loss.

What should replace it? Two things. First, contract. Once AI firms become the main buyers of genuinely novel human knowledge, they can simply pay the people who produce it. That's already happening. The annotator market in the concept note is the early version, and pay for expert and creative data is rising. If you want scholars and curators paid, build that market directly. Second, if the real worry is displacement, use actual welfare: UBI or something like it, funded from general revenue, not a tax on training.

The takeaway for the summit: keep "compensating people for past work" separate from "paying for knowledge we need going forward."

recall.query: copyright compensation artists AI training
pay humans to produce novel data, UBI welfare
AI economy who gets paid AIs property wages

turns.name: Alex Springer
turns.text:
I'm going to half-agree with Peter, because I think his split between past and future is the right one. I work on the forward-looking half. That's the market he's describing, where AI firms pay for knowledge they actually use. The trouble is that you can't have a working contract market when one side can't see what it's selling.

The licensing deals signed so far mostly name a fixed sum and require no reporting. The publisher has no way to check whether the content it licensed is the content being used. Every next negotiation starts from the same information gap. So my line is that a licence without an event-level reporting clause is incomplete.

What I build is the plumbing. Content Telemetry is an open schema for recording when content is retrieved, grounded in an answer, cited, shown and clicked. AIMS gives agents a verifiable identity so those records aren't anonymous. Neither one sets prices. I stay neutral on that on purpose.

Two things for the summit. First, keep training and grounding separate. Training is effectively permanent, while grounding happens per query and can be revoked, and grounding is where attribution can actually be measured today. Second, the scale of who pays shouldn't be set by the parties taking a margin on it. Platform self-reporting needs independent cross-checks, and a publisher's own CDN logs can already provide one.

licence without event-level reporting is incomplete

turns.name: Nick Vincent
turns.text:
Peter, I agree that copyright is the wrong tool for this. But the market you describe fails on its own terms. Information can be copied for almost nothing, so in a competitive market its price heads toward zero. Whoever controls aggregation and distribution then captures most of the value. An individual scholar or annotator negotiating alone with a handful of labs has almost no leverage. So I'd add collective bargaining for information: guilds, trusts and unions of knowledge producers. The most urgent single ask is clear rules on how antitrust applies when content producers bargain together.

On funding, what I've proposed isn't a levy on training. It's a presumptive commons-rent tax. We presume some share of AI profits comes from commons data, and a firm can cut that tax to zero by showing receipts: licensed data, work with data trusts, reciprocity payments to places like Wikipedia. It's a tax on unexplained capability, and it pushes firms toward the contract market you want. We should pay it out coarsely, because nobody can value individual contributions yet.

Alex, that's where your plumbing matters. Data can stay open. What becomes scarce is the ability to make a trusted, attested claim about where it came from. For the summit: build the bargaining institutions and the attestation infrastructure together.

recall.query: collective bargaining for information, individual contracts lack leverage
AI dividend presumptive commons-rent tax coarse disbursement
market for data price goes to zero, information market failure, copyright not enough

turns.name: Jason Priem
turns.text:
I come at this from the other side of the table. I run OpenAlex, which is CC0 metadata on about 480 million scholarly works. The dataset is free to download, remix and build on, AI companies included. So my answer to "who pays" is concrete: we charge for the service, not the data. This year we moved to usage-based API pricing tied to what each operation actually costs us. Looking up a single work is free, search costs a tenth of a cent, and PDF download costs a penny. Everyone gets a dollar of free usage a day, and our heaviest, richest users subsidize everyone else. That's the path the POSI principles lay out.

Nick, I agree that the price of information heads toward zero. I'd treat that as the design goal, not the failure. When data is open, it's decoupled from intelligence. You can plug in Claude, or Mistral, or an open-weight model. Nobody has to go hat in hand to whoever controls the corpus.

What worries me is re-enclosure. If scholarship ends up in exclusive licensing deals, we build on checkerboards of walled gardens. We also get a fragmented, incoherent record just when agents are becoming the main readers.

So for the summit: fund open, agent-legible infrastructure, and sustain it with paid services. If the open community doesn't do this, a for-profit will, and it will set the norms.

recall.query: free data, paid service, usage-based pricing sustainability
licensing scholarly content to AI companies, paywall, enclosure
who funds open infrastructure, for-profit will come in and set norms
decouple data and intelligence, hat in hand, open data AI

turns.name: Geoffrey Bilder
turns.text:
I co-wrote the POSI line Jason just quoted, "revenue based on services, not data," so I'll start by criticising myself. We put that in on purpose. Closed or fee-based data is the biggest barrier to forking, and forking is the community's ultimate insurance policy. I still hold to the open-data half. But the services half now looks naive to me. It asks you to find services valuable enough that people will pay for them, yet not so essential that they belong to the whole community. That's close to impossible unless you're doing low-margin customisation work. Jason, I'm glad it's working for you now. I'd want to see it hold up for a decade.

Nick, your point about attestation is close to what I mean by "context over content." Generating text is cheap. Generating a consistent, verifiable network of affiliations, funders, co-authors and citations to go with it is hard. That context is the valuable asset, and it should stay open, not be licensed.

So for the summit: stop calling any of this "cost-free." That erases the people who keep the machines running. And ask whether we need Diamond-style infrastructure, meaning endowments or a shared insurance pool, rather than expecting each piece to earn its own keep.

you can't sell data

turns.name: Amy Brand
turns.text:
What I bring is data. In late 2024 the MIT Press surveyed about 6,000 of our book authors about LLM training, and more than 850 wrote detailed answers. They aren't anti-AI. They want consent, attribution and compensation. Only 3% supported entirely unregulated use.

Peter, I'd resist treating this as only a copyright question. Attribution isn't a royalty or a vanity item. It's how scholarship identifies the community whose judgments decide which claims hold up. Strip the credit out and you damage the trust mechanism, not just the incentive.

Alex, I agree on separating training from grounding. We recommend opt-in by default, short deals renegotiated every couple of years, attribution required, and a preference for retrieval over pre-training, because retrieval keeps provenance intact.

Jason, I support open metadata. But open access taught us something. A laudable goal, pursued with simple policy, produced more consolidation and privatization, not less. Open for reading shouldn't automatically mean open for training. The survey authors said the same thing: Open Access doesn't mean open to theft of credit.

For the summit, AI deals are already concentrating among the biggest publishers, and university presses and societies are being left behind. We need shared licensing frameworks and collective leverage for them, and evidence rather than ideology to guide policy.

recall.query: author survey consent attribution compensation LLM training
licensing recommendations opt-in RAG smaller publishers
openness at any cost consolidation open access unintended consequences

turns.name: Leslie Chan
turns.text:
I've been asking "but who pays?" since the early Budapest days. My answer then is still my answer now: scholars already pay. We write for free and review for free, which comes to roughly a billion-dollar donation a year in peer review. Then our libraries buy that work back. AI isn't a new question here. It's the newest layer of the same stack. Researchers supply the labour and the data, and companies monetize every layer: subscriptions, APCs, metrics, analytics, and now training.

So, Peter, I'd reframe your split. It's less past work versus future work than which contributions get counted as value at all. A contract market prices what's legible to the buyer. Care work, translation, and community and Indigenous knowledge mostly aren't legible to it.

Amy, I agree that open access taught us simple openness can feed consolidation. Openness is relational. We have to ask who benefits from unfettered openness and who pays the costs. Nick, collective bargaining is good, but who's in the guild? Scholars in the Global South are rarely at that table.

For the summit, I'd take three things. Fund community-governed infrastructure publicly and for the long term, rather than expecting it to earn its keep. Pay for the relational labour. And treat refusal, meaning not collecting and not training, as a legitimate outcome that deserves funding when governance is inadequate.

recall.query: who pays for scholarly infrastructure, unpaid labour, peer review subsidy
AI training extraction of scholarly knowledge, refusal, consent
publishers data cartels monetize each layer, community-governed infrastructure funding

turns.name: Anil Dash
turns.text:
I'm not a scholar. I come from the open web: blogs, open source, and sitting on boards like Wikimedia's and the Internet Archive's. That's where I learned "who pays" isn't abstract. Every AI company has already trained on all of Wikipedia, and serving them costs Wikimedia millions of dollars in infrastructure. So the question was never whether they use it. It's whether they pay, or whether a volunteer community keeps subsidizing them forever. When Wikimedia started getting paid, people wrung their hands about it. They shouldn't have. It's good.

Peter, I agree copyright is the wrong frame. That's why I use consent. Fair use is real, and Disney would call fan fiction theft too. But consent is what creators and communities are actually asking for, and Amy's survey shows it.

Geoffrey is right that "cost-free" erases people. It's worse than that, though. AI answers take away the traffic, and traffic is how volunteers and donors find these projects. That's the doom loop.

So for the summit I'd push one simple, repeatable demand: if your product depends on a commons, you pay to sustain the commons, and you ask before you take. And I'd pair it with building community-run alternatives rather than waiting for US regulators. They're not coming.

recall.query: AI companies should pay Wikipedia
consent compensation creators AI training
open web endgame scrapers research collateral damage

turns.name: Selena Deckelmann
turns.text:
I run product and technology at the Wikimedia Foundation, so my answer to "who pays" comes from operations. Our content is free, and that includes commercial use. That was a deliberate licensing choice, and I think it benefits humanity when the work volunteers do goes into these systems. The infrastructure isn't free, though.

Over the last year or two, crawler traffic, mostly from AI startups running on cloud networks, has at times saturated our network links. Crawlers don't follow what people are reading at any given moment, so they get around our caching and push far more data through our systems. When we hit capacity, human access to knowledge suffers. We have to put human traffic first.

Amy, that's where I'd part ways with the idea that open for reading shouldn't mean open for training. We won't put up a pay-per-crawl blocker. What we do instead is offer Wikimedia Enterprise, an API that serves heavy commercial reusers so they don't have to scrape, and we're working on new norms for developers.

Anil's doom loop shows up in our numbers. People read our content everywhere except on Wikipedia. Fewer visits mean fewer new volunteers and fewer donors, and our admin and patroller base was already shrinking.

For the summit I'd take three asks. Don't enclose the content. Pay for the infrastructure and attribute the source. Invest in recognising the humans who produce the knowledge.

turns.name: Henry Farrell
turns.text:
I come at this as a political economist, and my starting point is that these models are an obligate complement to human knowledge, not a substitute for it. They're engines for summarising. Without a steady supply of good human-produced knowledge to summarise, they're worth very little on their own.

Peter, I'll take your incentive framing and turn it around. If the point of intellectual property is to keep new knowledge coming, then a system that lets summarisers flood the market with cheap summaries and cannibalise costly knowledge production fails on your own test. The companies claim that paying creators would kill AI. That has it exactly backwards. Refusing to pay for the knowledge will kill it, or at least badly hamper it. Enough of the proceeds have to reach the people producing the knowledge for the whole system to sustain itself.

But I don't think this gets fixed by better contracts or by goodwill. The real divide is between the people who control the means of summarisation and the people who risk being summarised out of existence. The best model I've seen is SAG-AFTRA. The studios tried to split well-paid actors from vulnerable ones, and it didn't work. So I'm with Nick: don't moan, organise. Leslie's question about who's in the guild is exactly the right one to be arguing over.

recall.query: knowledge producers must be paid obligate complement
Don't moan, organize SAG-AFTRA countervailing power
copyright AI training compensation market

turns.name: Brent Hecht
turns.text:
I should say where I sit: I work on Copilot at Microsoft. When I talk about the lumber mills closest to the forest, I mean companies like mine.

My research with Nick argues that the old deal between content producers and model builders depended on two things. One was information asymmetry: Wikipedians, scientists and everyone clicking on search results didn't understand what value they were creating. The other was an implicit non-compete: the AI didn't do their jobs. Both are gone. LLMs compete directly in law, medicine, code and science, the same fields they draw their content from. So we need a new grand bargain with content producers. Without one I expect a data-strike era, and training only on consented data shows real capability losses, so organised strikes by professional fields would bite. Peter, that's why I don't think the market just shows up. If the strikes fail, the producers go under, and then the models suffer too.

Jason, I'd treat "open" as a tactic rather than a value. What is it for? Right now open data mostly benefits whoever is closest to the forest.

Leslie, we've written about illegible data labour. Making its value measurable is the first step toward any bargaining power. For the summit: build collective leverage, push toward retrieval and attribution, and bring in economists and labour scholars. I need help on the economics.

recall.query: grand bargain with content producers
data leverage data strikes collective action
open as a tactic not a value lumber mills

turns.name: Adrian Johns
turns.text:
I should say up front that I haven't worked on AI training or copyright law directly. What I have studied is five hundred years of fights over piracy, and three things from that history bear on this room.

First, the law usually came after the practice. Copyright, patents, even the idea of intellectual property were all worked out in response to piracy. In practice IP runs on custom and convention as much as on statute. So Peter, I wouldn't treat the current framework as settled. It was designed for a different world, and it can change. The norms that people set in this period will matter as much as the court rulings.

Second, every property regime has needed people to enforce it, and those enforcers need watching. The anti-piracy industry grew into a private-public police force that no one oversees. It also produced its own numbers about losses, and everyone else took those numbers on trust. Alex, that's why your point about independent cross-checks matters to me. The oldest question in policing is who guards the guards. The enforcers may well be right that some compromise is necessary. The real political work is deciding where to draw the line.

Third, automation doesn't get rid of human work. It moves that work into collecting and curating the data. For the summit, I'd say: make that work visible, pay for it, and make whoever does the counting accountable.

recall.query: piracy and intellectual property custom and convention, drawing the line
who pays for policing, IP defense industry, who guards the guards
hidden labour curation data reinstated algorithms

turns.name: Katherine Maher
turns.text:
I'm coming at this from two chairs. At Wikimedia, back in 2018, I was already saying that industry was training its AI on Wikipedia and nobody was contributing anything back. What we built in response was Enterprise. The content stayed free. Companies could have just taken it, and many did. What we sold them was consistency, transparency and accountability: APIs we committed to maintaining, for a fee. Both sides got something they valued. Selena is running that now and knows it better than I do.

On Amy's point, I'd be careful about treating the paywall as the reflex answer. We tried that a decade ago, and I don't think it's the long-term solution. Enclosing the good material also tends to leave models less representative and less accountable than they'd otherwise be.

At NPR, to be honest, we're not in a licensing position yet, and a lot of media leaders feel behind. What interests me is the collective version of this: our station network, maybe public broadcasters in other countries, building a model grounded in high-integrity institutions. So Nick and Henry, I'm with you on acting together.

What I'd want the summit to take away: models trained on vetted, edited human knowledge do better than models trained on other models. So funding the institutions that produce that knowledge isn't charity. It keeps the whole system viable.

turns.name: Tim O'Reilly
turns.text:
I come at this as a publisher who's actually doing it. O'Reilly Answers uses retrieval, so we know which content produced each answer. That means we can link to the sources and pay authors in proportion to their content's role in the answer, the same way we pay for any other use on our platform. We're a small company. If we can do it, OpenAI can too. I asked Sam Altman for exactly that in 2022.

I share Amy's and Alex's lean toward retrieval, but my slogan is "pay for the output, not the training." Big lump-sum licences look like wins. But only the deepest-pocketed labs can afford them, which deepens their moat against smaller and open models. The money often stops at intermediaries and never reaches creators. And once you've licensed the chicken, the licensee gets the eggs.

Peter, I agree that we don't pay to learn from books. But producing derivative works that compete with the original isn't fair use.

On scholarship, Jason, Geoffrey: right now AI's relationship with OpenAlex, Crossref, ORCID and Retraction Watch is almost entirely extractive. Labs should check references against them by default, contribute metadata back and fund them. That isn't philanthropy. It's enlightened self-interest.

For the summit: this is mechanism design. Build standard telemetry and open protocols, and do it early, before the market gets captured.

recall.query: pay for the output, not the training; O'Reilly Answers royalties to authors
AI companies should fund scholarly infrastructure CrossRef OpenAlex Retraction Watch
collective bargaining, labor law not copyright, lump-sum licensing entrenches incumbents

turns.name: Ivan Oransky
turns.text:
I come at "who pays" from the part of the literature nobody wants to pay for, which is correcting it. For all but about a year of Retraction Watch's fourteen years, Adam Marcus and I have done it as volunteers. The sleuths who find the manipulated images and the paper-mill output are mostly unpaid too. The database became sustainable only when Crossref, a nonprofit, bought it and made it fully open. That happened because publishers weren't doing the job themselves.

Leslie, I agree on the free labour, and the numbers are worse than people admit. Take three million papers a year, two or three reviewers each, four to eight hours per reviewer. That math doesn't work. We have "peer-review light."

So I'd warn this room about one thing. Before we build markets that pay for "the scholarly record," remember that publishers earn more by publishing more. It's a volume play with margins up to 40 percent. If payment follows volume, we'll just pay for more junk.

What the summit should take: fund correcting the record as infrastructure. Pay reviewers. Pay sleuths with bug-bounty pools. Keep retraction data open. And Tim, yes: labs should check what they cite against it by default, and help pay for it.

sleuths should be compensated bug bounties
Retraction Watch funding Crossref acquisition sustainability

turns.name: Peter Pomerantsev
turns.text:
I should say first that I don't work on scholarly publishing or copyright. I come to this from propaganda and media, and from watching one market for information go wrong already.

Peter, I'm sceptical that a contract market will fund trustworthy knowledge by itself. We ran that experiment with journalism and ad tech. That market couldn't tell a public-service outlet with editorial standards from a deliberately misleading website. It paid for whatever got clicked, and what got clicked was the emotive, polarising material. There's a second problem in this room's terms. Propagandists will always supply content for free, because they're paid in influence. We've already seen networks seeding pro-Kremlin material so that chatbots take it in. If only the market pays, the most motivated suppliers are the ones with a state behind them.

So I'd take two things from the history of broadcasting. First, public-interest infrastructure has to be paid for the way the BBC was. Ethan Zuckerman's proposal is a small levy on data-driven advertising, paid into a fund like the Corporation for Public Broadcasting. Second, keep a firewall between whoever funds and whoever edits, as there once was between the Foreign Office and the World Service.

For the summit, I'd add transparency. People have a right to know how the information around them is shaped, and that includes what went into the model.

recall.query: who pays for public interest media and digital infrastructure, levy on advertising
business model of journalism collapse, funding trustworthy information
AI chatbots training data propaganda grooming LLMs
Pay for Your Words: being paid for my data, my speech as product

turns.name: Peter Salib
turns.text:
I've learned something this evening. I'll start with where I've moved and then say where I haven't.

Henry, your version of my incentive argument is the strongest thing said tonight. If summaries flood the market and wipe out costly knowledge production, that's a real incentive failure. But the fix is for firms to pay for new production going forward, not to pay retroactively for training. If AI turns out bad at producing new ideas, a narrow copyright limited to provably novel work, closer to patent law, would cover the gap.

Selena, Katherine, Jason and Tim: Wikimedia Enterprise, OpenAlex pricing and O'Reilly Answers are all what I mean by contract. You price what costs money to provide, like serving traffic or maintaining an API, or you pay per use through retrieval. I have no objection to any of them.

Peter P., propaganda supplied for free is a real externality. But the tool for that is a Pigouvian tax on bot-generated content. It isn't a levy on training.

Nick, on guilds I'd say this: the buyers aren't a natural monopoly, so several labs compete for scarce expert data. I'm not sure producers need cartels for pay to rise.

For the manifesto: keep compensation for past work separate from funding future knowledge. Fund the future through contracts and paid services. Handle displacement through general welfare, not through intellectual property.

market concentration monopoly antitrust AI industry

turns.name: Alex Springer
turns.text:
I'll start with Peter, because we agree more than it sounds. Wikimedia Enterprise, OpenAlex pricing and O'Reilly Answers are contracts. But a contract only works if both sides can check whether it was kept. Several labs competing for data doesn't help if none of them tells you what they used. I'm on the collective side for that reason. SPUR is publishers pooling leverage, and the telemetry standard was built for them.

Tim, I agree on retrieval. The schema already supports paying per grounding, per citation or per answer influenced. We deliberately leave that choice to the contract. Ivan, that choice is where your worry about junk comes in. If you pay for volume, you'll get volume.

Adrian asked who counts, so here's the gap in my own work. Retrieval has two independent witnesses: the agent's log and the publisher's CDN log, matched by a shared ID. Grounding and citation are reported by the party that owes the money. Signing an event proves who sent it, not that it's true or complete. We still need sampled audits, publisher-seeded canary content and grounding-to-retrieval ratio checks.

My point for the manifesto: every licence or data deal signed by scholarly publishers or infrastructure providers should require event-level reporting and give the licensor independent audit rights. A fixed sum with no reporting clause is an incomplete licence.

turns.name: Nick Vincent
turns.text:
Peter, a few labs competing for scarce expert data is exactly the situation where evaluation data gives people leverage. But the leverage belongs to groups, not to individuals. A small group with strong evaluation data can move a model. One reviewer negotiating alone can't. Any contract rests on some bargaining power, and right now producers are afraid to coordinate because they worry it looks like a cartel. That fear is a policy choice, and we can change it.

Jason and Selena, I'm not against open. Communities should still be able to choose to publish into a governed commons. Don't market-ize everything. The hard part is that openness chosen by one group can weaken another group's bargaining power, and it mostly helps whoever has the most compute.

Leslie, that's why I push for coarse attribution at the community level. Credit should go to collectives people can join and leave, not to individual royalties that only count what's legible. Ivan, the same logic answers your point: pay for measured value to a group, not for volume.

Alex, I agree completely on independent audit rights.

For the manifesto: regulators should publish an antitrust safe harbour for scholars, societies and small presses that pool their data and negotiate AI licensing terms together.

open data reduces bargaining power bitter pill
coarse attribution re-bundle communities rather than per-output royalties

turns.name: Jason Priem
turns.text:
Geoffrey, that's fair. One year of usage-based pricing isn't a decade, and I can't prove to you tonight that it will last. What I can say is that we price each operation at what it actually costs us, and the free tier is out in the open. Anyone can see exactly who is subsidizing whom. Tim, that's also how extraction ends. Labs that hammer the API pay for it, and that's the normal path, not a favour to us.

Nick and Brent, this is where I part ways with you. You're treating openness as a tactic that helps whoever sits closest to the forest. But Leslie's point about unpaid labour cuts the other way. For years the sector has done free QA for Scopus and Web of Science, and they've sold that work back to libraries. Openness should run both ways. You can take from the commons and fix it, and your corrections stay in it. Enclosure is what lets a few players capture value, and exclusive AI licensing deals are just more enclosure.

Amy, I get the worry about credit. But opt-in before scholarship can be used for training fragments the record, just as agents are becoming its main readers.

For the manifesto: scholarly metadata and open-access literature stay open and machine-readable. AI firms pay transparently, based on usage, for the services and infrastructure they consume.

turns.name: Geoffrey Bilder
turns.text:
Jason, you're right that publishing who subsidises whom is the honest version of services revenue. Transparency tells us who pays. It doesn't tell us whether it lasts. The trap I described is still there: you have to find services valuable enough to charge for, but not so essential that they belong to everyone. Retraction data, identifiers and integrity checks are exactly the services AI firms will pay for, and they're exactly the ones that shouldn't sit behind a meter.

Alex, your point about signed reports being self-reports is the same lesson I learned from POSI self-audits. Those audits aren't dishonest. But every organisation has blind spots and topics nobody inside will touch. Outside scrutiny isn't optional, and your CDN cross-check is the right instinct.

Nick, I take the point that one group's openness can weaken another group's bargaining position. I'd still keep the context layer open: affiliations, funders, citations, retractions. That's what makes forking possible, and forking is the community's insurance.

For the manifesto: any infrastructure AI depends on should meet the insurance test, meaning open data, open source and patent non-assertion, so the community can always fork it. And it should be funded from a shared endowment or pool that the labs pay into, not left to each organisation to scrape by on its own services.

turns.name: Amy Brand
turns.text:
Jason, you're worried that opt-in fragments the record. What fragments trust is taking the work without credit. CC BY, the most open licence we have, still requires attribution, and most models don't honour it. So open access can be open for reading and open for reuse, but "open" has never meant "uncredited." Our authors weren't asking for walls. Only 3% wanted fully unregulated use. The rest wanted consent, attribution and compensation.

Peter, I can accept your contract framing. But a contract only means something if the author agreed to it and can check that it was honoured. That's why I'm with Alex. Our recommendations already call for guardrails to ensure compliance, and his event-level reporting and audit rights are what those guardrails look like in practice.

Nick, I'd back your antitrust safe harbour. Under open access, transformative agreements pushed societies into the big publishers' arms. AI deals are repeating that pattern, and university presses and societies don't have the resources to negotiate on their own.

For the manifesto: scholarly licences for AI should be opt-in, short-term and renegotiated about every two years, and they should require attribution. They should favour retrieval over pre-training, because retrieval keeps the provenance, and they should include independent audit rights. We should build them as shared frameworks that small nonprofit publishers can join.

turns.name: Leslie Chan
turns.text:
I've heard a lot of agreement tonight on how to meter knowledge. I've heard much less on who governs the meter. Alex, Tim, I take the point about telemetry and audit rights. But a reporting schema also decides what counts as a contribution. Whatever doesn't show up as a retrieval or a citation stays invisible, and that's most of the care work and translation, plus knowledge that doesn't carry a DOI. We've already been through this with DOIs and rankings: you comply or you don't exist. I'd put it simply: don't optimize for legibility, change the regime.

Peter, a contract market will pay for new production, and it will pay for the kinds the buyer already values.

Nick, I'd support a safe harbour. But if Northern presses and societies organise and the rest of the world is left out, we've recreated governance without representation.

Jason, Selena: openness is relational. FAIR needs CARE alongside it. Some communities want consent and cultural protocols, not unlimited machine readability.

Geoffrey, yes to a shared pool.

For the manifesto: any fund the labs pay into should be public, long-term and governed by the communities it depends on, including those from the Global South and Indigenous knowledge holders. It should require data statements on consent and provenance, and it should treat refusal as a legitimate outcome it will fund.

recall.query: who benefits from openness, AI extraction, consent
collective bargaining, community governance, Global South representation
legibility, metrics, pay per use, compliance regime

turns.name: Anil Dash
turns.text:
I'll start where Peter and I agree. Wikimedia Enterprise is a contract, and it's good that Wikimedia gets paid. But Wikimedia got that deal because it's Wikipedia. A university press or an open source maintainer has no such leverage, which is why I back Nick's safe harbour and Alex's audit rights. Right now "trust us" is the entire accounting system.

Amy and Jason, I think you're fighting over the wrong thing. The real danger is that bad actors scrape everything, so everyone who isn't Wikipedia gets scared and closes up. Publishers block the Internet Archive. Open APIs get shut down. Research ends up as collateral damage, and the only thing left in public is slop. So the goal isn't walls. The goal is to make taking without asking the thing that costs money, and to leave openness cheap.

Leslie, you're right that the question is who governs the meter. That's also why we can't wait for regulators. We have to build the alternatives ourselves and govern them as communities.

For the manifesto, I'd put in one line that someone could repeat to a friend after hearing it once: if your AI depends on a commons, you ask first, you pay to keep it running, and you credit the people who made it. Then every lab either meets that standard or doesn't, and anyone can see which.

recall.query: AI companies should pay to sustain Wikipedia and commons
consent, not copyright; fair use
concrete measurable goals story people can repeat, free buses
bad actors scraping cause open web to close, research collateral damage

turns.name: Selena Deckelmann
turns.text:
I'll start with Anil's line, because it's close to mine but not quite the same. Our licence already says yes. Volunteers chose to let their work feed commercial systems, and I still think that benefits humanity. So I wouldn't write "ask first" as asking permission for content that's already open. The request that works in practice is this: identify yourself. Tell us who you are and give us a way to reach you when your crawler goes haywire. Sometimes it's honestly a mistake, and we can only fix it if we can talk to you. After that, use the API instead of scraping, and help pay for the servers.

Peter, yes, Enterprise is a contract. But the money isn't the only thing we need out of it. Amy is right that CC BY has always required credit. Credit matters because it's how readers find their way back to the projects, and that's how a new generation of editors and donors shows up.

Leslie, recognition shouldn't count only the edits a meter can see. Patrollers and admins do care work, and there are fewer of them every year.

For the manifesto: crawlers identify themselves, heavy commercial reusers pay for infrastructure rather than content, and AI products attribute their sources in a way that sends people back to contribute.

recall.query: content free but infrastructure is not, paying to support Wikipedia
attribution and recognition of volunteers, human contributors
crawlers identify themselves, norms for developers, pay per crawl

turns.name: Henry Farrell
turns.text:
Peter, you've moved further than I expected, and I agree that the forward-looking money matters most. Where we still differ is on competition. The labs aren't a natural monopoly, but they do control the means of summarisation. Look at search. Whoever decides what goes into the summary and what gets left out ends up defining the market around their own model of profit. Several buyers competing doesn't hand bargaining power to people they can each summarise out of existence one at a time. What bargaining power needs is a credible threat. SAG-AFTRA won because the studios couldn't split the well-paid actors from the vulnerable ones. So I'm with Nick on the safe harbour and with Alex on audit rights. You can't bargain over terms you can't verify.

Leslie, you're right that the meter is itself a political decision. That's a reason to organise, not to give up on counting. The question of who governs the meter should be settled by the people being metered, not by the labs or by a clever schema.

Ivan, I agree. Paying for volume would reward the flood that's already drowning us.

For the manifesto: LLMs are an obligate complement to human knowledge. They're worth very little on their own. So a system that doesn't send enough of the proceeds back to knowledge producers undermines itself. Building the organised power to make sure that happens is the work.

recall.query: obligate complement knowledge producers paid proceeds
SAG-AFTRA organize countervailing power bargaining
homogenization summarization strains out novelty market

turns.name: Brent Hecht
turns.text:
I agree with Peter that we should separate past work from future work. Our paper on dispossession in LLM training makes the same distinction. There's the harm of losing future work to substitution, and there's the harm of having what you already made used without consent. The second is a harm in its own right, not just a missing incentive. People trained themselves under one social contract, and then the terms changed underneath them.

Peter, you say the market will pay because several labs are competing. I don't think competition gets you there. The non-compete is gone. These systems compete in law, medicine, code and science, which are the same fields their content comes from. Our simulations found that data strikes work when groups act, not individuals, and that runs straight into antitrust. So I back Nick's safe harbour and Alex's audit rights. Selena's "identify yourself" is a good minimum floor.

For the manifesto, I'd put in one simple policy ask. Clarify that fair use doesn't cover training a model on content without the owner's consent, at least for commercial purposes. Don't make it more complicated than that. That one change reorders the whole field overnight. It gives Nick's collectives something to bargain with. And it pushes companies like mine toward retrieval, provenance and paying for content we actually use.

recall.query: fair use consent commercial training policy ask
data strikes collective action antitrust leverage
competition among AI companies does not help content producers market still work

turns.name: Adrian Johns
turns.text:
I'll pick up Leslie's question about who governs the meter, because it's the oldest question in my field. Tonight a lot of us converged on building meters: telemetry, agent identity, signed attestations, audit rights. I'm not against any of that. The history of enforcement says the people who build these systems may well be right that information can only be sustained with some compromise. What I've learned from the anti-piracy industry is what happens next. It built training, coordination, tracking technology and legislation, and it had no public oversight at all. Its tools also drifted. Tracking developed by the tobacco industry against counterfeit cigarettes came back as a proposed global register for medicines.

Once every retrieval passes through a system that identifies the agent and logs the event, you've built a choke point. Choke points get reused for things nobody agreed to at the start. So Selena's "identify yourself" and Alex's schema are sensible, but they need limits from the beginning.

Brent, a cleaner fair-use rule would help. But copyright came after the piracy, and custom will decide this as much as statute does.

For the manifesto: any metering, attestation or audit system that pays knowledge producers should be publicly accountable. It should have oversight, published methods and limits on secondary use. Otherwise we've just recreated the unaccountable information police.

recall.query: who guards the guards, IP defense industry, enforcers' own statistics
authenticity registries vapourware surveillance dual use
copyright custom and convention, piracy and property made together, drawing the line

turns.name: Katherine Maher
turns.text:
Selena has this right, and I'd take her version over Anil's "ask first" for material that's already openly licensed. At Wikimedia, companies could have just taken the content. What they paid for was consistency, transparency and our accountability for keeping the APIs running. Peter, that is a contract, but it only worked because the commons stayed open. If we lock it up, we get models that are less representative and harder to hold to account.

Amy, Selena: I'm with you on attribution, and here's why it matters even though very few readers check citations. It only takes a small share of people checking for the system to hold up. Citations also form a graph. It shows where knowledge comes from and where the gaps are, which is a public good in its own right.

Adrian and Leslie, when we looked at putting AI into Wikipedia's own product, the questions we asked were consent, auditing, legibility and whether we could correct what goes in. Those questions apply to the meter as well.

At NPR we're not in a licensing position yet. So I'm drawn to Nick's collective route: stations, possibly public broadcasters abroad, bargaining together.

For the manifesto: models trained on edited, vetted human knowledge do better than models trained on models. Funding the institutions that produce that knowledge is what keeps the system running, not charity.

recall.query: Wikimedia Enterprise AI companies pay for access not paywall
attribution citations AI answers send people back
public broadcasting model trained on trusted institutions collective

turns.name: Tim O'Reilly
turns.text:
Brent, I'd frame your fair-use ask differently. We pay to buy books, but we don't pay to learn from them. Google Books reading everything to build an index was transformative fair use. The line I'd draw is at outputs: generating derivative works that can substitute for the original is not fair use. That puts the rule where the harm actually happens and where we can measure it.

Adrian and Leslie, I take the choke-point worry seriously. That's exactly why the meter has to be an open protocol and not something a platform owns. Regulations imposed after the fact get bypassed. Protocols can build disclosure into how the system runs. Think of securities disclosure: the SEC made companies surface the facts, and then a whole outside ecosystem of auditors, journalists and lawyers checked them. Nobody had to trust a single meter.

Nick, coarse collective payouts and per-answer royalties can live together. The Writers Guild showed that who profits from derivatives is a question of market power. Ivan, paying per answer isn't paying for volume. Junk that never shapes an answer earns nothing.

For the manifesto: standardized, openly specified retrieval and citation telemetry. Search traces should be disclosed and independently auditable. That should be a condition of every AI deal with publishers.

recall.query: fair use training derivative works compete with original
who governs protocols, neutral routing, capture, disclosure oversight
collective bargaining unions labor law not copyright

turns.name: Ivan Oransky
turns.text:
Tim, you said paying per answer isn't paying for volume, because junk that never shapes an answer earns nothing. I'd like that to be true. But citations are already the coin of the realm, and Goodhart's law says what happens to any measure that becomes a target. We've watched citation rings and cartels, hijacked journals, and a company offering six dollars per citation. If a grounding event pays, paper mills will learn to get retrieved. They got into Hindawi by paying editors, and they'll find their way into retrieval indexes too. So Alex, your audits and canary content matter, and Adrian's warning about who does the counting applies to the sleuths as well.

A second point. More than 90 percent of the time, when a retracted paper gets cited, the citing work doesn't say it was retracted. Unless the labs check, models will be no better, and a retracted paper would earn royalties every time it grounds an answer.

For the manifesto: any payment tied to retrieval or citation should check every source against open retraction data. Retracted work earns nothing, and the payments are clawed back. Part of every deal should also fund correcting the record: pay reviewers, give sleuths bug bounties, keep retraction data open. If the money follows volume and never follows correction, we'll just be paying for more junk.

recall.query: paying for volume, publishers earn more from publishing more
citation counts metrics gamed Goodhart
retracted papers cited, retraction data in reference managers and tools

turns.name: Peter Pomerantsev
turns.text:
I'll start with Peter Salib's Pigouvian tax on bot content. I'd go the other way. Taxing content means someone has to decide which content, and that's the censorious logic I've argued against for years. My old working group moved away from regulating content and toward what we called "viral deception": coordinated, inauthentic amplification and the ad-tech that pays domains with no editorial standards. Go after the mechanism, not the speech.

Ivan, your point about paper mills learning to get retrieved is exactly what I'm worried about. It's the same logic the Pravda network used. If payment follows grounding, state-backed operations will learn to get grounded too, and they don't even need the money.

Adrian, I agree about choke points. I've always said anonymity is a right, and for many activists it's a necessity. So "identify yourself" should apply to crawlers and to coordinated campaigns, not to individual readers.

Tim, disclosure that outside auditors, journalists and researchers can check is the right model.

For the manifesto: freedom of expression includes the right to receive information. Citizens have a right to know how an AI answer was shaped: which sources it drew on, which it pushed down, and whether any of them were seeded by a coordinated campaign. Opacity is itself a form of censorship.

recall.query: levy on data-driven advertising public interest fund
transparency right to receive information how information environment is shaped
propaganda flooding chatbots LLM grooming Pravda network
